lines: A probabilistic step sequencer played from a grid controller, giving four trigger outputs and two control voltages
Sets the internal clock, from a 2 second period at fully counter-clockwise to a 47ms period at fully clockwise
A general-purpose control whose job depends on what the grid is showing: hold a grid key standing for a continuous value and turn this to edit that value
Short-press to open the preset view on the grid; press and hold to save the current state into the active preset slot
Click to reclaim a grid that has been taken by another module; the right-click menu is where a grid is first chosen
A clock for the sequencer; each rising edge above 2.21V advances it one step, and the width of the incoming pulse sets the length of the trigger outputs
A gate at the current clock rate, following the internal clock or the external one as appropriate
One of four trigger outputs, 0V low and 8V high, firing on the steps set for it on the grid
A control voltage, 0V to 10V, stepping through the values set for it on the grid; quantized to the nearest semitone unless the grid is in curves mode
A control voltage, 0V to 10V, stepping through the values set for it on the grid; quantized to the nearest semitone unless the grid is in curves mode
Note — this module does nothing but run a clock until a grid is connected. Add a grid module or attach a hardware grid, then right-click here and pick it from the Device Connection list.
Note — once a sequence has been entered from the grid, the grid can be disconnected and the sequence keeps playing.
Note — inserting a patch cable into the clock input with nothing at the other end stops the sequencer.
Note — a hardware grid needs serialosc installed; a virtual grid module needs nothing.

whitewhale.notes: The panel prints its labels in lower case: param, clock, in, out, A, B and the numbers 1 to 4. The USB jack is a Rack switch parameter and so can be mapped with VCV MIDI-MAP or Stoermelder MIDI-CAT to move a grid between modules from a controller. The clock knob's range, 2 seconds to 47ms, and the trigger level of 8V come from the maker's manual in docs/content/modules/whitewhale.md and docs/content/general/voltage.md. The Switch Firmware menu offers the Kria alternate firmware as well as the standard one.

The maker names the knobs and their outputs SHAPE 1 to SHAPE 3 in the tooltips and CV 1 to CV 3 in the manual. teletype.notes: Teletype's trigger outputs go to 10V, not the 8V the plugin's general voltage page gives for TR outs elsewhere; both figures are the maker's own, on docs/content/modules/teletype.md and docs/content/general/voltage.md respectively. The trigger inputs are the one place in the plugin where a rising edge is acted on immediately rather than at the downsampled input rate, which the maker's voltage page calls out as the exception. Two shortcut menu items are present in the source but commented out — a GRID visualizer mode and a system variables toggle — so they are not written here. The input index order is IN first, then TRIGGER 1 to 8; the panel puts the eight trigger jacks across the top with the in jack at the right of the first row.

lines: A multi-mode sequencer and voltage generator whose personality changes with the app it is running, giving four triggers and four control voltages
A key whose job depends on the running app: a long hold opens the time view in Kria and Meadowphysics, a short tap steps to the previous pattern in Earthsea and Levels, and it adds friction in Cycles
A key whose job depends on the app: a long hold opens the config view in Kria, Meadowphysics, Cycles and Levels; a short tap gives the next pattern in Earthsea, a pattern reset in Cycles and Levels
Short-press to open the preset view; press and hold to rotate through the apps available with the connected device, which the lamp beside it shows by colour
Click to reclaim a grid or arc that has been taken by another module; the right-click menu is where a device is first chosen
A trigger input whose job depends on the running app: a clock in Kria, Meadowphysics, Earthsea and Levels, and friction in Cycles
A trigger input whose job depends on the running app: a reset in Kria, Meadowphysics, Cycles and Levels, a pattern start and reset in Earthsea, and force in Cycles when the first input is patched
One of four trigger outputs, 0V low and 8V high, driven by the running app
One of four control outputs, 0V to 10V, driven by the running app
Note — this module does nothing until a grid or an arc is connected. Add a grid 64, grid 128 or grid 256 module, or attach hardware, then right-click here and pick it from the Device Connection list.
Note — the five apps are Kria, Meadowphysics, Earthsea, Cycles and Levels; the first three need a grid, the last two an arc. The hardware MIDI and Teletype expander modes are absent here.
Note — once an app is running the device can be disconnected and the app keeps running, answering the panel keys and the two inputs as before.
Note — the lamp beside the mode key names the running app by colour: yellow-orange is Kria on a grid or Levels on an arc, white is Meadowphysics or Cycles, and yellow-white is Earthsea.
Note — to hold one of the panel keys down with a mouse, control-click it on Windows or Linux and command-click it on a Mac; it stays down until you click it again.
Note — the reset follows the Nord protocol: only a clock edge advances the sequence, and a reset going high makes the next clock step start it again. Delay the clock if a reset misses.

lines: A 16 by 8 grid of keys that a white whale, earthsea, meadowphysics, ansible or teletype connects to as its control surface
One key of the grid; its brightness is set by the module the grid is connected to, and pressing it sends that key's position to that module
Note — this module has no jacks and produces no voltage. Place it in the patch, then right-click a white whale, earthsea, meadowphysics, ansible or teletype and pick this grid from its menu.
Note — connecting this grid to a second module unplugs it from the first. Clicking the USB jack on a module reclaims the grid for that module.
Note — control-click a key to hold it down while the control key stays down, so several keys can be held at once; on a Mac use command-click. Releasing the control key releases them all.
Note — control-shift-click a key to lock it down until you click it again; on a Mac use command-shift-click. A locked key carries a dot in its lower left corner.
Note — Rack has no multi-touch, so gestures the hardware performs with two hands are done here by holding or locking keys with the modifier keys.

Menu — Mirror hardware grid — mirrors a connected hardware grid onto this one, with a Stop mirroring item to end it

Menu — Protocol: 40h, Series, Mext (varibright) — sets which generation of grid this one emulates; Mext is the one to leave it on, the other two match older hardware without variable brightness
Menu — Release Locked Keys — releases every key that has been locked down, which pressing Escape with the mouse over the grid also does
grid128.notes: Each key is two parameters: an even-indexed one carrying the key itself and an odd-indexed one for MIDI mapping (src/virtualgrid/VirtualGridModule.cpp:90-108). Only the even-indexed parameters are given a widget (src/virtualgrid/VirtualGridWidget.cpp:97), so only those can be clicked; the odd ones get no line and no tag. The maker's parameter names are wrong throughout: the naming loop computes its index as i + j * w * 2 while the widget uses (i + j * w) * 2, so the tooltip on key (1,0) reads (2,0) and most of the names are either doubled or blank. One line covers every key because they are identical. The module has no inputs and no outputs.

grid64.notes: Each key is two parameters: an even-indexed one carrying the key itself and an odd-indexed one for MIDI mapping (src/virtualgrid/VirtualGridModule.cpp:90-108). Only the even-indexed parameters are given a widget (src/virtualgrid/VirtualGridWidget.cpp:97), so only those can be clicked; the odd ones get no line and no tag. The maker's parameter names are wrong throughout: the naming loop computes its index as i + j * w * 2 while the widget uses (i + j * w) * 2, so the tooltip on key (1,0) reads (2,0) and most of the names are either doubled or blank. One line covers every key because they are identical. The module has no inputs and no outputs; 128 of the parameters are unreachable.

lines: A 16 by 16 grid of keys that a white whale, earthsea, meadowphysics, ansible or teletype connects to as its control surface
One key of the grid; its brightness is set by the module the grid is connected to, and pressing it sends that key's position to that module
Note — this module has no jacks and produces no voltage. Place it in the patch, then right-click a white whale, earthsea, meadowphysics, ansible or teletype and pick this grid from its menu.
Note — connecting this grid to a second module unplugs it from the first. Clicking the USB jack on a module reclaims the grid for that module.
Note — control-click a key to hold it down while the control key stays down, so several keys can be held at once; on a Mac use command-click. Releasing the control key releases them all.
Note — control-shift-click a key to lock it down until you click it again; on a Mac use command-shift-click. A locked key carries a dot in its lower left corner.
Note — Rack has no multi-touch, so gestures the hardware performs with two hands are done here by holding or locking keys with the modifier keys.

lines: Sixteen faders with sixteen voltage outputs, modelled on the 16n hardware controller, which also serves as a parameter expander for teletype
Sets the voltage on the output below it, over whichever range the menu has chosen
The voltage of the fader above it
The voltage of the sixteenth fader, or all sixteen fader voltages on one polyphonic cable when polyphonic mode is on
Note — placed immediately beside a teletype, this becomes a parameter expander: the FADER operator reads its sixteen faders as whole numbers from 0 to 16383, whatever voltage range is set here.
Note — to drive these faders from a 16n or another MIDI controller, pick the device on the MIDI connection submenu. The default mapping is continuous controllers 32 to 47 on channel 1.
Note — this module has no inputs.
Menu — Fader voltage range: 0-10V, 0-5V, +/-5V — sets the range every fader covers
Menu — Fader size: 90mm, 60mm — sets how long the faders are drawn, the shorter setting leaving room below them for labels
Menu — Polyphonic mode — turns the sixteenth output into a polyphonic cable carrying all sixteen fader voltages
Menu — MIDI connection — chooses the MIDI driver and device the faders follow
Menu — Autodetect 16n configuration — interrogates a connected 16n for its controller and channel mapping and matches the faders to it; with none present it resets to controllers 32-47 on channel 1

faderbank.notes: The outputs are created without configOutput, so they have no names in the module browser or in a tooltip; the panel numbers them 1 to 16. Only the sixteenth output can be polyphonic, and only while Polyphonic mode is checked (src/faderbank/FaderbankModule.cpp:32-43). The maker's manual calls the size menu item 'Fader length'; the source prints 'Fader size' (src/faderbank/FaderbankWidget.cpp:176), and the lines follow the source. The range field is left off the output props because the voltage range is a menu setting rather than a fixed fact.
